The majorant optical depth shift maps a medium interaction depth $t$ sampled on a base viewing segment to a corresponding depth $t'$ on a target viewing segment [S1].

The claim states that the majorant optical depth shift maps a medium interaction depth $t$ from a base segment to a corresponding depth $t'$ on a target segment. Source [S1] explicitly describes this process in Appendix B, deriving the mapping equation $t' = C * ( ar{mu}_{n_l} /  ar{mu}'_{n_{l'}}) * t + R$ based on the equality of majorant optical depths ($ ar{	au}'(t') = C *  ar{	au}(t)$). The notes and passages confirm that this technique is used to map depths between segments to enable path reuse, accounting for geometry and extinction differences. Every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported

Find the index $n_{l'}$ such that $t'_{\min, n_{l'}} \le t' < t'_{\max, n_{l'}}$ in the target segment [S1]. *Note: $t'$ is initially unknown.

The claim describes a specific step in the algorithm derived in Source [S1]: finding the index $n_{l'}$ corresponding to the target depth $t'$. The source text explicitly defines $n_{l'}$ (denoted as $n_{t'}$ or $n_{l'}$ in various parts of the derivation) as 'the volume section index containing depth $t'$ on the target segment'. By definition, if $n_{l'}$ is the index of the volume section containing depth $t'$, then $t'$ must lie within the entry and exit depths of that section, i.e., $t'_{min, n_{l'}} < t' < t'_{max, n_{l'}}$ (or inclusive depending on boundary conditions, but the inequality holds). The source confirms this definition and the context of the derivation where $t'$ is the variable being solved for or mapped. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim that one must find this index to satisfy the geometric constraints of the volume sections.

- $\bar{\tau}_{\max}$: The total majorant optical depth of the base segment (sum of $\bar{\mu}_j (t_{\max, j} - t_{\min, j})$ for all $j$) [S1].

The claim defines $ ar{	au}_{	ext{max}}$ as the total majorant optical depth of the base segment, calculated as the sum of $ ar{mu}_j (t_{	ext{max}, j} - t_{	ext{min}, j})$ for all $j$. The evidence in Source [S1] defines the majorant optical depth $ ar{	au}(t)$ using a piecewise summation. Specifically, the total optical depth corresponds to the case where $t$ is at the maximum exit depth of the last segment. In this context, the term $ ar{mu}_j (t_{	ext{max}, j} - t_{	ext{min}, j})$ represents the optical depth contribution of the $j$-th volume section. The derivation equations (Eq. 26 and the definitions of $a_1, a_2$) rely on these section-wise sums. The constant $C$ is defined as $ ar{	au}_{0,	ext{max}} /  ar{	au}_{	ext{max}}$, implying $ ar{	au}_{	ext{max}}$ is the total majorant optical depth of the base segment. The formula provided in the claim matches the standard definition of the total optical depth for a piecewise constant medium derived from the summation of section contributions.
